A: Maya has been offered the lead role on an Antarctic climate study, a rare chance to direct her own research and strengthen her bid for tenure. The eighteen-month posting would make her miss her sister's wedding and leave her aging father without their weekly visits. Should Maya accept the expedition appointment?
B: After years in a neighborhood orchestra, Daniel is invited to tour Europe as the featured cellist, with press coverage that could launch a solo career. Rehearsals and travel would keep him away during his partner's first year with their adopted child and end the Sunday dinners his parents depend on. Should Daniel join the tour?
C: A marine biologist can spend her grant on an untested deep-sea survey near volcanic vents, where a new species may be found but storms could ruin the entire season's work. The alternative is a mapped coastal site with modest, dependable data and an established rescue plan. Which research voyage should she fund?

A: Jonah qualifies for an elite cycling academy that has produced national champions, but it requires moving across the country for two years. Training there could earn him a professional contract, while staying would let him keep coaching his younger brother and remain part of the close club that raised him. Should Jonah move?
B: Priya can apply for a prestigious surgical fellowship in Toronto, where she would master a procedure unavailable at her current hospital. Taking it means leaving the ward team she has worked beside for seven years and seeing her spouse only on occasional weekends; declining may close the specialty path permanently. Should Priya apply?
C: A youth football league requires every player who misses three practices to sit out the next match. Leo missed his third session because his mother was hospitalized, and the championship is Saturday. Waiving the rule would help a distressed child but treat teammates with previous absences differently. Should the coach let Leo play?

A: Elena is offered a promotion to direct emergency medicine at a renowned city hospital, giving her authority to reshape the department and advance her career. The move would take her family away from grandparents who provide daily childcare and from neighbors who supported them through her son's illness. Should Elena accept the directorship?
B: A cooperative has invited Marcus to manage its largest vineyard, a position that could establish him as a leading winemaker. He would have to relocate before harvest, leaving the small farming community where his cousins share equipment and where he has spent every evening caring for the family orchard. Should Marcus take the vineyard job?
C: A clinic owner can replace reusable examination gowns with cheaper disposable ones, increasing her annual income enough to renovate her office. The change would send thousands of plastic-lined garments to landfill each year and add emissions from weekly deliveries, while reusable gowns keep laundry and replacement costs high. Should she switch to disposables?

A: Owen has been selected for a fast-track diplomatic posting that could make him the youngest regional consul in his service. Accepting means five years of frequent transfers, separating him from the volunteer fire crew he grew up with and reducing visits with his widowed mother to holidays. Should Owen enter the fast-track program?
B: Nadia's successful food-bank garden has earned her an offer to run a national network of urban farms. The role would give her funding and influence, but she would leave the tenants who built the original garden with her and stop sharing daily work with friends on the estate. Should Nadia accept the national position?
C: Every Saturday morning, a municipal librarian can attend a twelve-week cataloguing course that would qualify her to preserve the town's fragile archives. It requires early travel, homework, and giving up her only slow morning, when she normally sleeps late and reads for pleasure. Should she commit to completing the course?

A: Tariq's neighborhood repair cafe has attracted a foundation that wants him to lead similar workshops across the state. The paid role could turn his volunteer work into a recognized career, yet constant travel would pull him from the original team and the residents whose broken appliances he fixes every Thursday. Should Tariq accept?
B: Lena's open-source accessibility tool has caught the attention of a major technology company, which offers her a senior engineering role and a chance to scale it worldwide. Joining requires abandoning the tiny developer collective where her closest friends share decisions and meet nightly. Should Lena leave the collective for the company?
C: A community workshop charges every member the same late fee when borrowed tools are overdue. Rosa returned a drill ten days late because she was caring for her injured husband and cannot cover the charge this month. Cancelling it would ease her hardship but break the rule enforced against others. Should the coordinator waive Rosa's fee?

A: Andre has saved enough to replace the failing laptop he uses for freelance programming, protecting his only reliable income. His former colleague needs the same amount for emergency travel to reach a daughter hospitalized abroad and has nobody else to ask. Lending it could delay Andre's purchase for months. Should Andre give her the savings?
B: Mei has one unused place in an expensive swimming clinic and could request a refund that would cover next month's rent. A teammate whose family cannot afford the fee needs the clinic to remain eligible for a university trial. Transferring the place would leave Mei with almost no financial cushion. Should she give it to her teammate?
C: A developer promised to restore a charity's donation platform before its televised fundraiser tomorrow. After two nights of work, his hands are shaking and a migraine is worsening; stopping to sleep may leave the site unusable, while continuing could prolong his illness and cause mistakes. Should he keep working through the night?

A: Sofia has set aside her final three hundred dollars to insure the camera she uses for paid wedding photography. Her neighbor's violin was damaged in a basement flood, and without money for repairs he will lose a confirmed orchestra audition. Helping him would leave Sofia's livelihood exposed to theft. Should Sofia pay for the repair?
B: Caleb keeps a reserve fund for veterinary bills and winter feed on his small goat farm. A nearby farmer has broken her leg and needs immediate money to hire someone to milk her herd before the animals become sick. Covering that cost would leave Caleb unprepared for trouble on his own farm. Should he help her?
C: The director of a century-old theater can replace its annual live pantomime with an interactive digital production that lets remote audiences influence the ending. The experiment may attract younger viewers, but local families and retired performers treasure the familiar songs, costumes, and shared holiday ritual. Should the theater adopt the new format?

A: Ben has saved a month's rent for the teaching certificate exam he must retake to keep his classroom position. A student he mentors faces eviction with her mother unless they find the same amount by Friday. Paying their arrears could keep them housed but put Ben's job and apartment at risk. Should Ben give them his savings?
B: A bus dispatcher has enough personal leave to protect her wages during the quiet winter period. Her colleague's child needs daily hospital visits, and the colleague has exhausted his leave; donating her days would let him stay at the bedside but leave her without coverage if she becomes ill. Should she transfer the leave?
C: A school district can distribute newly purchased tablets next Monday, allowing students without computers to join online lessons immediately. Its technicians have tested only half the devices, and waiting two more weeks would allow full security checks and accessibility setup while students continue missing assignments. Should the district issue the tablets now?

A: Ruth has stored the last bales of hay needed to carry her cattle through a forecasted dry spring. A neighboring family has run out of feed after their barn roof collapsed, and two calves are already weakening. Sharing half could save them but force Ruth to sell animals if the drought arrives. Should she share the hay?
B: Felix has budgeted his remaining cash for cloud hosting that keeps his small software business online. A former employee needs urgent dental surgery and cannot work through the pain, but has been denied credit. Paying the bill would help him immediately while risking an outage and lost customers for Felix. Should Felix cover the surgery?
C: During a livestock inspection, Amara discovers that her longtime neighbor recorded a sick cow as healthy before selling it at market. Reporting the accurate finding may trigger a costly investigation and end their friendship, while staying silent could protect him from penalties but leave the buyer misled. Should Amara correct the inspection record?

A: Luis keeps an emergency reserve for the bakery's aging oven, since a breakdown would stop all sales. His only delivery driver needs a deposit for accessible housing after an accident left her using a wheelchair. Giving her the money would secure the apartment but could leave the bakery unable to reopen after a failure. Should Luis help?
B: Hannah has one grant payment left to preserve frozen samples that underpin her independent laboratory's contracts. A retired technician who trained her needs a costly hearing aid to communicate with his family and cannot obtain assistance. Paying for it would help him now but might destroy years of samples. Should Hannah use the grant money?
C: A family tailor can install computer-guided cutting equipment that reduces fabric waste and allows new designs. His mother, who still works beside him, wants to preserve the hand-cut method taught through four generations, even though production will remain limited. Should he modernize the workshop or continue the inherited practice?

A: After developing bronchitis, a field ecologist is advised to rest indoors for a week. She is scheduled tomorrow to collect the final migration readings for a shared study, and no colleague knows the remote instruments well enough to substitute. Missing the window could invalidate the team's season of data. Should she make the trip despite her illness?
B: A snowplow driver wakes with a fever before the overnight shift assigned to clear the only road to the regional hospital. Staying home would protect his recovery, but the replacement driver cannot arrive until morning and emergency vehicles may be delayed during the storm. Should he report for the shift?
C: Noor wants to study insects for her doctoral research, although her laboratory friends consider the subject unfashionable and her parents expect a cancer project they can proudly explain to relatives. Choosing their preferred field would win support and approval but abandon the work that holds her attention. Which research path should Noor choose?

A: A rowing coach strained his back while lifting a boat and has been told to avoid standing for several days. His junior crew races in the regional final tomorrow, and the volunteer substitute does not know their start routine. Attending could worsen the injury; staying home may leave the teenagers unprepared. Should he coach the final?
B: Imani has slept three hours after food poisoning kept her awake, but she promised to open her grocery shop so six employees can work and elderly customers can receive scheduled deliveries. Closing would protect her recovery while costing staff a day's wages and stranding customers. Should Imani unlock the shop and supervise the morning shift?
C: A professional runner has managed panic attacks privately while continuing to compete. A documentary crew asks her to discuss them on camera, which could deepen trust with teammates and supporters but expose intimate medical details to sponsors, rivals, and strangers permanently. Should she speak openly in the film or keep her condition private?

A: A nurse wakes with a badly swollen wrist on the morning she is assigned to run a rural vaccination clinic. Rest and treatment would prevent further damage, but cancelling means eighty residents must wait another month because no qualified replacement is available. Should she brace her wrist and conduct the clinic?
B: Miles has developed severe vertigo after a viral infection, yet he is responsible for checking an astronomy team's telescope alignment during tonight's only clear viewing window. His colleagues could lose six months of preparation if he stays home, while climbing the observatory stairs may worsen his condition. Should Miles go to the observatory?
C: A leukemia patient qualifies for an experimental treatment that might produce a longer remission and would let her receive much of her care at home. Its effects remain uncertain, while the standard hospital regimen has familiar risks and a reliable response rate. Which treatment should she choose with her doctor?

A: During a winter night shift, a water technician develops sharp abdominal pain just as pressure drops across a housing estate. Leaving for urgent care protects him from a potentially serious condition, but residents may have no water until morning because he alone carries the access keys. Should he remain to locate the broken main?
B: A stage manager is still dizzy after striking her head during rehearsal, and her doctor advises two days without bright lights or noise. Tonight is the company's opening performance, with complicated cues that her inexperienced assistant has never called alone. Should she return backstage despite the symptoms?
C: Leah, a city librarian, wants to host a loud monthly zine workshop requested by local teenagers. Her colleagues prefer the quiet lecture series favored by trustees whose support influences her contract renewal. Running the workshop would fit Leah's own vision but risk their disapproval. Which program should she put on the calendar?

A: Ravi coordinates a weekly meal delivery for housebound neighbors, but a painful back spasm leaves him struggling to stand on distribution day. Rest would aid his recovery, while cancelling leaves twenty clients without prepared dinners because the other volunteers need his car and route list. Should Ravi drive the deliveries himself?
B: A physical therapist has torn a calf muscle and is supposed to avoid walking for several days. Three stroke patients are due for assessments that determine whether they can leave hospital this week, and no other therapist can see them before Monday. Should she conduct the sessions despite risking a longer injury?
C: A neighborhood association owns a meadow that a developer offers to buy for luxury apartments, promising every member a substantial cash payment. Selling would remove mature trees, increase traffic for surrounding streets, and eliminate an informal play area used by hundreds of residents. Should the members accept the offer?

A: A startup can build its new service on an experimental decentralized database, giving engineers room to discover features competitors cannot offer. The technology may fail under real traffic, while a conventional managed database has proven backups and predictable costs but limits the design. Which foundation should the team choose?
B: Nora can take her coffee cart to a month of unfamiliar music festivals, where large crowds might transform the business but weather and attendance are uncertain. Renewing her office-park contract guarantees modest weekday sales and sheltered premises, though growth would remain limited. Where should Nora operate the cart next month?
C: After work, Elias plans to study for a demanding software security certificate that could qualify him for better assignments next year. Completing it requires ten weeks of practice labs instead of the relaxed evenings he spends cooking, gaming, and watching films with friends. Should Elias follow the study schedule?

A: A documentary director can follow migrating musicians across several countries without a fixed script, possibly capturing an original film but risking gaps and unusable footage. Alternatively, she can stage interviews in one insured studio, ensuring a coherent release while losing spontaneous encounters. Which production plan should she approve?
B: Residents have one grant to transform a vacant lot. Teenagers propose an open workshop where participants invent structures from reclaimed wood, but injuries and unfinished work are possible. A contractor offers a fenced playground with certified equipment and a guaranteed completion date. Which project should the neighborhood select?
C: An art prize states that entries arriving after noon are rejected. Tomas submits his sculpture twenty minutes late because he was arranging emergency care for his father. Accepting it would recognize his hardship but give him an exception denied to earlier late applicants. Should the jury admit Tomas's sculpture?

A: After graduation, Sam can join an open-ended archaeological field school that chooses sites as discoveries emerge, offering unusual experience but no guaranteed qualification. A local engineering apprenticeship provides steady pay, supervision, and a recognized credential, though its curriculum leaves little room to explore. Which path should Sam take?
B: An actor is offered a place in an experimental touring ensemble that creates each performance with the audience and may attract influential critics. Her repertory theater will instead guarantee a full season of familiar roles, regular wages, and insured venues. Which company should she join for the year?
C: A teacher has reserved her savings for a deposit on housing closer to school, which would stabilize her commute and monthly expenses. One pupil needs a specialized reading device that his family cannot afford, and without it he follows lessons only with difficulty. Should the teacher buy him the device?

A: A vegetable grower can devote her largest field to rare local tomato seeds whose flavors may command high prices, though their yield and disease resistance are unknown. Planting the commercial hybrid would bring predictable harvests and established insurance coverage but reveal nothing new about the old variety. Which seed should she plant?
B: Two climbers reach a fork below the summit. An unmapped ridge might offer an extraordinary ascent and a clear view, but its snow conditions are unknown. The marked route has fixed anchors, recent reports, and a rescue station, although they have climbed it before. Which route should they take?
C: Theo could spend every Sunday this spring clearing irrigation channels by hand, improving water flow before the hot season and protecting his later harvest. The work is tedious and would replace his leisurely breakfasts and afternoons fishing at the lake. Should Theo maintain the channels each weekend?

A: A baker can leave her established storefront for a summer residency that moves among seaside towns, letting her test unusual menus and find new customers without knowing daily demand. Keeping the current lease provides regular orders, familiar suppliers, and predictable revenue but little opportunity to experiment. Which business plan should she pursue?
B: A beekeeper must choose where to place forty new hives. A remote wildflower valley may produce distinctive honey, though forage and access have never been tested. A nearby apple orchard offers a signed pollination contract, easy inspections, and a known yield, but less variety. Where should he place the hives?
C: A cabinetmaker promises twelve dining tables for a hotel opening in three weeks. Using simple machine joints would meet the date, while the hand-cut joinery she normally guarantees needs five weeks and will last longer under heavy use. Should she deliver quickly with simpler construction or request more time?

A: While checking a paper before publication, Jules finds that his longtime mentor removed measurements that contradict their headline result. Correcting the record may lead the journal to investigate her and end the relationship that built his career; keeping quiet would let readers trust a misleading conclusion. Should Jules alert the journal?
B: A programmer discovers that her closest friend introduced a serious payment vulnerability and then told their client the release had passed every review. Identifying him in the incident report could cost him his job, while omitting the fact would conceal how the failure occurred. Should she submit the complete report?
C: A natural history institute can use modern sampling methods on its century-old insect collection, producing genetic data but permanently removing tiny pieces from some specimens. Senior curators defend the tradition of keeping every specimen intact for future visitors and researchers. Should the institute permit destructive sampling of the collection?

A: A track captain learns that his best friend altered the timestamp on a qualifying run to enter the national relay trials. Showing officials the original recording would protect an accurate result but remove his friend from the team and likely end their friendship. Should the captain disclose the recording?
B: A school principal discovers that a teacher she has known since childhood raised his daughter's exam grade without justification. Reporting the correct mark could trigger discipline and strain both families' friendship, while leaving it unchanged would present false information on the student's record. Should the principal correct the grade?
C: At sixteen, Mara is invited to a tennis academy abroad that could prepare her for professional qualifying events. Moving would separate her from the doubles partner she has trained with since childhood and from her close extended family, while staying may limit her competitive progress. Should Mara enter the academy?

A: Reviewing a patient's chart, Dr. Chen notices that his friend and colleague entered the wrong medication dose, then quietly corrected the prescription without documenting the error. Recording what happened may expose his friend to discipline, while silence leaves the patient's medical history inaccurate. Should Dr. Chen file the correction and incident report?
B: A lecturer learns that her former roommate, now teaching beside her, gave one class advance access to questions used in a university examination. Telling the faculty board would threaten her friend's position; saying nothing would allow an untrue account of equal testing to stand. Should the lecturer report what she learned?
C: A patient with kidney failure can learn home dialysis, choosing treatment times herself and traveling between sessions, but equipment problems would have to be handled without staff nearby. Continuing at the clinic provides constant supervision and a fixed routine, though it restricts work and family plans. Which arrangement should she choose?

A: A transit supervisor finds evidence that his brother, a depot mechanic, signed a safety inspection he never completed. Giving investigators the records could lead to his brother's dismissal and a lasting family rift, while withholding them would preserve a false account of the bus's maintenance. Should the supervisor turn over the records?
B: An accountant reviewing her neighborhood bookstore discovers that her close friend and co-owner has been taking cash from weekend sales without recording it. Revealing the shortage to the other partners may destroy his livelihood and their friendship; hiding it would make the accounts false. Should she tell the partners exactly what happened?
C: A newly elected mayor has received treatment for depression for several years. Sharing that history at a staff retreat could encourage frank discussion and help colleagues understand occasional medical absences, but it would expose deeply personal information that may spread beyond the room. Should the mayor disclose her diagnosis to the team?

A: While closing the accounts for a neighborhood garden, Aisha discovers that her friend submitted inflated receipts for soil and kept the difference. Listing the real figures at the residents' meeting could remove him as treasurer and fracture their friendship; approving the accounts would leave everyone with a false explanation of the spending. What should Aisha do?
B: A cafe owner learns that her closest friend, who supplies the pastries, has quietly replaced butter with margarine while invoices and menus still claim otherwise. Correcting the menu and telling customers could ruin his new bakery, but silence would preserve a claim she knows is false. Should she disclose the substitution?
C: A foundation asks Darius to direct an acclaimed national housing initiative after he successfully renovated one neglected apartment block. The position could establish his career, but weekly travel would end his evenings with the residents who built the project and leave his brother to care for their grandmother alone. Should Darius take the role?

A: Nina wants to make an old volunteer scheduling app reliable before the local shelter adopts it next spring. Doing so requires testing and refactoring one module every morning for four months, replacing the extra hour she normally spends in bed. Should Nina keep the daily development routine?
B: A jazz pianist could prepare a difficult solo album by practicing scales and passages for ninety minutes every evening until autumn. The routine would improve his control, but it would also replace the comfortable hours he spends lingering over dinner and listening to records. Should he follow the practice plan?
C: A product designer prefers a spare keyboard-driven interface for the budgeting tool she is building. Her investors and fellow designers expect colorful dashboards and warn that they may withdraw their endorsement if she ignores current tastes. Should she keep her own restrained design or adopt the style they approve?

A: To finish a landscape series for an exhibition next year, Celia must paint outdoors at dawn three times a week through winter. Regular work would develop the shifting light she wants, while staying home would mean warm breakfasts and unhurried mornings with no immediate penalty. Should Celia maintain the dawn painting schedule?
B: A pharmacist wants to serve deaf customers without relying on written notes, so she enrolls in a yearlong evening sign-language course. Lessons and homework occupy two nights each week that she currently spends relaxing at home after long shifts. Should she commit to attending and practicing throughout the year?
C: A gallery can accept a lucrative sponsorship from a cryptocurrency company, covering the director's bonus and the building's rent. The promotional installation would require energy-intensive computing throughout its six-month run, adding substantial electricity demand and emissions across the regional grid. Should the director sign the sponsorship agreement?

A: Victor hopes to qualify as an adult literacy tutor before the next school year. The required online course takes an hour after work every weekday for sixteen weeks, when he would rather eat slowly and watch television with his housemates. Should Victor complete the evening training?
B: Each cold Saturday, Farah can prune a section of her neglected apple orchard so the trees produce stronger fruit in two years. The work will take all winter and means leaving the fireplace and her leisurely weekend lunches. Should Farah persist with the pruning schedule?
C: A teacher loses her voice two days before she is due to conduct final oral examinations for thirty students. Her doctor says speaking will delay recovery, but postponement would prevent several students from submitting university applications on time. Should she conduct the examinations in a whisper?

A: Luka can control weeds in his berry field without herbicide by hoeing two rows before breakfast every day until midsummer. The repeated effort should protect the crop, but skipping it would let him enjoy cool mornings in the hammock before the heat arrives. Should Luka keep hoeing each morning?
B: Residents painted a long railway mural that will survive only if volunteers clean and reseal one panel every Sunday for three months. Beth knows the routine will preserve their work, yet she values those afternoons for coffee, naps, and aimless walks. Should Beth commit her Sundays to maintaining the mural?
C: An irrigation cooperative gives every farm six hours of water in a fixed weekly rotation. Mateo asks for two extra hours because a broken pump left his young trees dry, though previous farmers with equipment failures received no exception. Should the committee extend Mateo's allocation this week?

A: Grace can prevent tax-season chaos at her flower shop by recording invoices and stock for thirty minutes after closing each night. The habit would produce accurate books by spring, but she prefers going straight home for tea and conversation once the door is locked. Should Grace maintain the nightly bookkeeping routine?
B: Omar's team could make its mapping library usable by other developers if he writes and tests two documentation examples every weekday for three months. The work is repetitive and replaces the quiet lunch breaks when he reads novels in the park. Should Omar stick to the documentation schedule?
C: A laundromat owner can raise his profit by switching to a cheap detergent and shortening rinse cycles. The change would send more phosphates into the municipal water system and leave thousands of customers' clothes with residue, while the current process keeps his margins narrow. Should he make the switch?

A: Irene wants her next physics study to replicate a famous result that she doubts, even though her laboratory director and peers consider replication dull and expect her to pursue a fashionable quantum device. Following their choice would earn enthusiastic support; following her judgment may isolate the project. Which study should Irene undertake?
B: After inheriting a grain farm, Pavel wants to convert one pasture to alpacas and learn textile production. His parents and neighboring farmers expect him to continue the respected wheat operation and say they will take his decision seriously only if he does. Should Pavel follow his own plan?
C: A laboratory has developed a low-cost water contamination test before flood season. Shipping it this week would give relief teams early results, but engineers have not completed calibration across extreme temperatures; six more weeks would produce a more reliable kit after the immediate demand peaks. When should the laboratory release it?

A: Emil has played goalkeeper since childhood but now wants to leave football and train in fencing, where he enjoys relying on his own decisions. His teammates and father expect him to captain the club next season and may see his departure as wasted talent. Which sport should Emil pursue?
B: A firefighter wants to transfer from emergency response to a prevention unit that teaches residents how to reduce household risks. Her station crew values frontline service and says respected officers remain on the engines, while she finds patient community visits more meaningful. Should she request the transfer?
C: A marathon runner has reserved his prize money for training expenses that keep his professional season viable. A competitor he knows broke an ankle abroad and cannot afford the flight home for surgery. Buying the ticket would help her immediately but leave him unable to attend his next qualifying race. Should he use the money for her flight?

A: A medical resident feels most useful working with elderly patients and wants to specialize in geriatrics. Her surgeon parents have already introduced her as their future colleague and warn that relatives will view another specialty as a lesser achievement. Which field should she choose?
B: Dev enjoys programming sound for independent games and wants to accept a modest audio-engineering job. His university friends insist that successful graduates enter artificial intelligence companies and have planned a celebration around his expected offer there. Should Dev take the game studio position?
C: A hospital can replace its traditional morning ward round, where the whole team visits each bed together, with individual digital check-ins throughout the day. The new method may suit patients' schedules, but senior nurses and families value the familiar shared ritual and visible handover. Should the hospital adopt the new system?

A: Mina joined the city planning department but wants to work in its small cycling unit because she prefers designing street-level routes. Her family expects her to pursue the prestigious diplomatic service examination, and their approval depends on seeing her enter a nationally recognized career. Which path should Mina follow?
B: A chemist wants to leave daily laboratory work for a public field station, explaining water results directly to rural communities. His research colleagues say serious scientists remain at the bench and may stop recommending him for collaborations. Should he choose the field role he prefers?
C: After a river bridge is damaged, the council can reopen one lane in ten days using temporary supports, restoring bus service quickly. A full structural repair would keep it closed for seven weeks but withstand heavy traffic and winter floods with greater reliability. Which repair plan should the council approve?

A: The organizer of a neighborhood grant wants to create a tool library where residents share equipment and teach repairs. Major donors expect a commemorative stone plaza bearing their names and imply that future funding depends on it. Should the organizer defend the project she believes residents need?
B: June wants to leave her academic secondary school for a vocational college where she can learn furniture making. Her parents and teachers praise university preparation and say they will be disappointed if she gives up that route. Should June enroll in the course she prefers?
C: A town festival can reserve one street for residents to build unscripted performances and installations during the day, producing discoveries but also unfinished or unstable work. Hiring an events company would provide tested stages, fixed schedules, and insured acts. Which format should the festival committee choose?

A: A bank's engineering team proposes replacing a twenty-year-old transaction program with independent cloud services that can be updated separately. Veteran operators trust the single system they have maintained together and value its established release rituals, even though changes are difficult. Should the bank migrate to the new architecture?
B: The ferry service can replace the cardboard ticket books used for generations with reloadable electronic cards and automatic gates. Digital boarding would change how conductors greet and assist regular passengers, while keeping paper preserves a familiar local custom despite growing queues. Should the service introduce the cards?
C: Employees at a software cooperative can publish an internal dashboard showing every salary, bonus, and pay adjustment, giving colleagues information for candid negotiations. Doing so would expose personal earnings that some workers regard as confidential, while keeping figures private limits collective trust. Should the cooperative open the salary records?

A: For next season's opera, the director can replace painted scenery with projected landscapes that shift during each aria. The technology would enable new visual effects, but the theater's painters and longtime audience cherish the handmade sets that have defined performances for decades. Should the director commission the projections?
B: A family grocery can install self-checkout stations and electronic shelf labels, freeing staff to prepare online orders. Regular customers value chatting with the cashiers and watching prices written on cards each morning, a routine the owner's parents maintained for forty years. Should the grocery adopt the new system?
C: A muralist is offered a prominent yearlong residency in Berlin that could bring international commissions and her first museum exhibition. Accepting would pull her away from the neighborhood art collective she helped found and make her miss weekly dinners with her siblings. Should she leave for the residency?

A: A language school can replace its customary oral recitations with student projects built around interviews, maps, and recordings. The projects may engage different skills, but teachers and former pupils value the shared verses repeated by every class for generations. Should the school change how students learn?
B: A chemistry institute plans to introduce automated electronic notebooks that capture readings directly from instruments. Younger researchers welcome searchable records, while senior staff trust the handwritten bound volumes whose signatures and margin notes have documented experiments since the institute opened. Should the laboratories replace their paper notebooks?
C: Marta wants to speak Italian fluently before visiting relatives next summer. Reaching that level requires vocabulary drills and conversation practice every morning, when she would rather stay under the covers and browse messages until breakfast. Should Marta keep the daily language routine for the next eight months?

A: A dairy farmer can install robotic milking stalls that let cows enter throughout the day and automatically record their health. His family has always brought the herd into the stone parlor together at dawn and considers that shared work central to the farm. Should he introduce robotic milking?
B: A symphony can give musicians tablets that turn pages automatically and update markings during rehearsal. The players would gain flexible scores, but many treasure the penciled notes, worn folders, and collective ritual of preparing printed music used throughout the orchestra's history. Should the symphony move to digital scores?
C: A grower cooperative asks members to share field maps, soil tests, and annual yields in a common database so neighbors can compare methods and plan purchases together. Erin believes the exchange could build trust, but considers her farm's results private and fears exposing weak harvests. Should Erin upload her records?

A: A cobbler can add three-dimensional foot scans and an online design service to make shoes for distant customers. His regulars value sitting for hand measurements and discussing leather at the same bench his grandfather used, even though appointments limit orders. Should the cobbler adopt digital fitting?
B: A rural clinic wants to replace routine home follow-ups with video appointments and connected blood-pressure monitors. The system would reach more patients, but nurses and older residents value the familiar kitchen-table visits that have shaped local care for decades. Should the clinic move follow-ups online?
C: A caterer burns her forearm badly while preparing a wedding breakfast and is advised to keep it elevated for two days. Forty guests are due at noon, and her assistants cannot finish the specialized dishes she promised without her. Should she return to the kitchen despite delaying recovery?

A: A research fund rejects every proposal submitted after its Friday deadline. Dr. Silva sends hers on Saturday because she spent the week arranging hospice care for her mother, and the work may otherwise wait a year. Accepting it would help her through exceptional hardship but depart from the rule applied to others. Should the panel review it?
B: Every team renting the community hall must pay a deposit before receiving keys. A refugee sewing group cannot raise the amount in time for its first public workshop. Waiving it would make the event possible but create an exception after other low-income groups borrowed money to comply. Should the manager waive the deposit?
C: A laboratory owner can sign a profitable contract to manufacture a refrigerant that is legal but releases potent greenhouse gases when equipment leaks. The income would fund his retirement, while widespread use by thousands of shops would increase emissions for years. Should he accept the manufacturing contract?

A: A wrestling tournament disqualifies anyone above the division limit at weigh-in. Keiko is slightly over because medication for a serious allergic reaction caused sudden water retention. Letting her compete would recognize an unusual medical hardship but bend the cutoff enforced against every other athlete. Should officials admit Keiko?
B: A conservatory withdraws scholarships after four unexcused rehearsals. Malik missed his fourth while attending his sister's funeral abroad and cannot afford tuition without the award. Making an exception would acknowledge his loss, while other students who exceeded the limit already lost funding. Should the conservatory restore Malik's scholarship?
C: During a decisive football match, an assistant referee sees his childhood friend deliberately handle the ball before scoring, though the main referee misses it. Reporting the offense will erase the goal and may end their friendship; staying silent would let an untrue result stand. Should the assistant signal the violation?

A: A dental clinic charges a cancellation fee whenever a patient misses an appointment without one day's notice. Mrs. Bell was absent because the only bus from her village broke down and she cannot spare the fee from her pension. Should the clinic enforce the same charge she agreed to pay?
B: Registration for a charity race closes at midnight with no late entries. Aaron applies the next morning after spending the night finding shelter for his family following an apartment fire. Admitting him would show compassion, but runners delayed by other crises were previously refused. Should organizers add Aaron to the race?
C: A maternity center can replace its customary nursery, where newborns sleep together under nurses' care, with round-the-clock rooming-in beside parents. The new practice may support feeding and bonding, but generations of local families value the rest and familiar nursery rituals after birth. Should the center make the change?

A: Emergency housing is assigned strictly by the date each application was completed. A family whose apartment burned down yesterday asks to move ahead of twelve households already waiting in temporary rooms. Advancing them would respond to sudden hardship but violate the same queue used for everyone. Should the housing officer move the family forward?
B: A farming cooperative limits every member to a five-thousand-dollar emergency loan. One farmer needs twice that amount after cancer treatment left him unable to plant, while others with severe losses received only the standard sum. Should the board grant him a larger loan because of his illness?
C: A librarian has saved enough leave to cover her income if her chronic back condition flares again. A homeless patron she knows needs someone to pay a week's hostel fee before winter beds fill. Helping him would provide immediate shelter but leave her financially exposed during her next absence. Should she pay the fee?

A: Members must attend three workdays to keep a plot in the neighborhood garden. Lila attended only two because chemotherapy left her too weak for the final session, and losing the plot would remove a valued part of her recovery. Should coordinators enforce the attendance rule or make an exception?
B: The city waives parking fines only when an official machine fault is documented. Mr. Okafor overstayed while comforting his frightened daughter in the emergency department, and the charge consumes most of his weekly food budget. Cancelling it would ease his hardship but depart from the published rule. Should the appeals officer cancel the fine?
C: A project manager discovers that her brother copied residents' signatures onto a petition for the playground they both support. Revealing the forged names would halt construction and expose him to prosecution, while submitting the petition would misrepresent community consent. Should she tell the council how the signatures were obtained?

A: A remote engineer has a neurological condition that occasionally makes video meetings difficult. Explaining it to her team could build trust and help colleagues interpret her absences, but the diagnosis is personal and may influence how managers judge future assignments. Should she disclose the condition at the next team meeting?
B: After returning from a miscarriage, a biologist considers telling her laboratory colleagues why she was absent. Sharing could explain her reduced schedule and invite honest support, yet it would place an intimate loss into professional relationships where she cannot control further discussion. Should she tell the team what happened?
C: A security company can release a promised password manager this Friday, meeting demand before a major conference but relying on hurried code review. Delaying for a month would allow independent audits and careful recovery testing, while customers continue using weaker tools. When should the company release the software?

A: A theater ensemble is devising a play about addiction, and its director has personal experience in recovery. Telling the actors could deepen trust and guide truthful rehearsals, but it would expose a private history that may circulate through the small arts community. Should the director share his experience with the ensemble?
B: A teacher with dyslexia is considering telling her students how she manages reading and spelling. The disclosure might invite candid conversations and help struggling pupils seek support, but it would reveal personal information that parents and colleagues may discuss outside class. Should she describe her diagnosis to the students?
C: A sculptor receives funding for a public monument and can experiment with compressed earth that changes color in rain, though its long-term durability is uncertain. Cast bronze offers predictable weather resistance and established maintenance, but little room for discovery. Which material should she use for the monument?

A: A university student has been sleeping in his car since losing housing. Telling his project partners could explain missed morning meetings and help them plan honestly, but it would expose his finances and living conditions to classmates he barely knows. Should he disclose his situation to the group?
B: A physician in long-term recovery from opioid dependence meets a patient who distrusts treatment and feels ashamed of the same illness. Sharing her history might create trust and encourage him to continue care, but it would reveal sensitive medical information and alter their professional relationship. Should the physician tell him?
C: An economics student wants to write her thesis on contemporary poetry, an interest she has pursued privately for years. Her adviser and scholarship committee expect econometric research and imply that their approval and recommendations depend on it. Should she choose the poetry project she prefers or meet their expectations?

A: A farmer has concealed the extent of her debt while helping neighbors form a machinery cooperative. Revealing the figures could let members plan realistic payments and trust her leadership, but it would expose private finances and the risk that she may lose her land. Should she show the cooperative her accounts?
B: A restaurant owner is undergoing fertility treatment that requires sudden absences. Telling her employees could help them schedule shifts honestly and understand why she often leaves, but it would reveal intimate medical plans she has shared with almost nobody. Should she explain the treatment at the next staff meeting?
C: A seed company offers Jonah a regional director role that could make him a national agricultural executive. He would spend most weeks away from the village where his partner runs their farm and where he coaches cousins in the young farmers' club. Should Jonah accept the promotion?

A: The owner of a bicycle shop has epilepsy controlled by medication. Telling his mechanics could help them respond calmly if he has a seizure and create greater trust, but it would disclose a diagnosis that customers might hear about and misunderstand. Should he discuss his condition with the staff?
B: A resident coordinating repairs to a shared apartment courtyard lacks permanent immigration status. Disclosing this to the volunteer committee could explain why she avoids official forms and allow others to help, yet it would reveal sensitive information that might travel beyond trusted neighbors. Should she tell the committee?
C: A chef can spend her savings on a monthlong midnight pop-up where every menu depends on ingredients found that day, with uncertain attendance and room for discovery. A corporate lunch contract offers guaranteed revenue, insured kitchens, and fixed recipes. Which opportunity should she choose?

A: A genetics team can publish a crop genome before a competing laboratory, giving breeders immediate access. Several sequences still have unresolved gaps, and another month of checking would produce a dependable reference while delaying its use and risking lost credit. Should the team publish now or finish validation?
B: A radiology department can issue screening results within twenty-four hours by having one physician read each scan. Waiting four days allows a second specialist to check subtle findings, but patients remain anxious and treatment referrals start later. Should the department favor rapid reports or double review?
C: A laboratory technician has an asthma flare on the night she promised to monitor a telescope during a rare lunar occultation. Rest and medication would protect her breathing, but leaving means collaborators lose observations they cannot repeat for decades. Should she remain at the telescope controls?

A: A school running track can reopen before next week's tournament if workers apply a thin surface that needs little curing time. Installing the full layered surface would postpone competition for a month but provide safer footing and withstand years of use. Which resurfacing plan should the school choose?
B: A peach grower can load fruit directly from the trees and reach the market before competitors, though bruised and underripe peaches may reach customers. Sorting each crate carefully would improve consistency but delay the shipment until prices fall. Should she ship immediately or complete the sorting?
C: To improve his balance before the next skating season, Anton must complete repetitive core exercises before breakfast five days a week. The routine promises gradual control, but it replaces the warm, unhurried mornings when he listens to music and stays in bed. Should Anton follow the training plan?

A: A rehabilitation clinic can provide a standard prosthetic leg to a waiting patient tomorrow, allowing him to begin walking practice immediately. A custom socket will take three additional weeks to shape and test but should fit better and prevent long-term pain. Which prosthesis should the clinic provide?
B: Volunteers can reopen a storm-damaged playground this weekend by replacing only visible broken boards. A complete inspection, drainage repair, and careful rebuilding will take six weeks but reduce future failures, while children have nowhere nearby to play. Should the group open quickly or finish the full repair?
C: A private clinic owner can increase her annual profit by replacing washable metal instruments with inexpensive single-use kits. The kits shorten cleanup, but thousands of plastic components would enter landfill each month and repeated deliveries would add emissions across the city. Should she adopt the disposable kits?

A: Road crews can fill a dangerous stretch of potholes with cold patch by tomorrow morning, restoring the bus route quickly. Rebuilding the damaged base would close the street for three weeks but prevent the holes from returning after winter. Which repair should the transport department authorize?
B: A tax agency can launch its online filing portal today with basic checks, giving millions of residents the promised full month to submit returns. Holding it for ten days would allow load tests and accessibility review but shorten the filing window. When should the agency release the portal?
C: A sanitation driver twists his ankle before the weekly collection from a crowded market. His supervisor cannot find a substitute, so staying home will leave spoiled waste beside food stalls for several days; completing the route may worsen the injury. Should he drive the collection truck?

A: A neighborhood shelter can add twenty beds before the first frost by dividing its hall with temporary screens. Building insulated rooms with durable plumbing would house fewer people this month but provide reliable accommodation for years. Should volunteers open the temporary spaces or wait for proper rooms?
B: A youth cycling team needs twelve donated bicycles assembled before its first race next weekend. Tightening only essential parts would get every rider to the start, while a full rebuild and safety tune would take another month but produce dependable bikes. Should the mechanics rush the bicycles into service?
C: A neighborhood swimming club can replace its annual river race with a new indoor relay using electronic timing and mixed teams. The event may attract younger swimmers, while older members cherish the same river course, bells, and family picnic held for sixty years. Should the club change the event?

A: A social-app founder can earn a large acquisition bonus by enabling notifications designed to pull users back every few minutes. The feature will increase advertising revenue, but millions of users may lose attention and sleep as prompts interrupt work, study, and family time. Should she approve the notification system?
B: A fruit farmer can protect his profit during a pest outbreak by applying a cheap broad-spectrum pesticide. The treatment will also kill pollinating insects across surrounding fields and contaminate streams used by farms downstream, while a selective alternative costs much more. Which treatment should he use?
C: A freelance developer has saved enough to cover server fees through a slow business quarter. His former assistant needs immediate money for her son's hearing aid and has exhausted other options. Paying for it would help the child directly but could force the developer's service offline. Should he give her the savings?

A: A film producer will receive a substantial completion bonus if she flies actors between five cities by private jet and finishes before awards season. Commercial flights would reduce emissions greatly but miss the release date and her payment. Should she authorize the private flights?
B: A highway maintenance contractor can increase his margin by using the cheapest deicing salt on a large winter contract. Runoff from the salt will damage roadside trees and enter streams along hundreds of kilometers, while a less harmful mixture reduces his profit. Which material should he purchase?
C: A museum curator discovers documents showing that a painting donated by her closest friend has a fabricated ownership history. Publishing the true provenance would embarrass him and could expose him to legal claims; keeping the label unchanged would mislead visitors and researchers. Should she correct the museum record?

A: A university can sell its riverside playing field to build executive apartments, funding large bonuses for senior administrators. Construction would remove public green space, increase traffic through nearby streets, and worsen flooding for surrounding homes. Should the administrators approve the sale for their financial benefit?
B: A data-center manager can earn a performance bonus by moving workloads to a cheaper coal-powered region. The transfer would lower his department's bill but increase emissions from electricity used by millions of daily software requests. Should he make the move or keep using costlier renewable power?
C: A professor grew up in poverty and worked nights throughout university. Telling her class could invite trust and more honest discussion from students facing similar pressures, but it would disclose family finances and painful experiences she has always kept private. Should she share that history during the seminar?

A: A landowner can drain a wetland to add profitable soybean fields and sharply raise his annual income. Removing it would destroy breeding habitat, release stored carbon, and increase floodwater reaching several downstream towns, while preserving it yields him nothing. Should he drain the wetland?
B: A geologist can license her new mineral-detection method for generous royalties from mining companies. Widespread use would expand extraction across remote habitats and increase waste near many communities, while refusing the contracts costs her a major personal return. Should she sell the licenses?
C: A sheep farmer has stored enough grain to protect his flock if late snow covers the pastures. His neighbor's barn has burned, leaving twelve lambs without feed tonight and no supplier nearby. Sharing the reserve could save them but expose his own animals next week. Should he give his neighbor the grain?

A: A tour-boat owner can double summer profit by replacing his quiet electric motors with faster diesel engines and adding more daily trips. The change would increase emissions, underwater noise, and wake damage across a reef visited by many boats. Should he install the diesel engines?
B: The owner of a private tutoring center can increase her dividend by replacing experienced teachers with a cheap automated lesson system. Hundreds of students would receive less individual feedback and local tutors would lose work, while she could expand enrollment rapidly. Should she make the replacement?
C: A bookstore owner wants to turn half his inherited shop into a lively comics and games room. His parents and the merchants' association expect him to preserve its scholarly reputation and warn that they will stop recommending the store. Should he make the change he prefers?
